01 · The problemWhy I built it

Plans that look right, but aren't

Wuhan is my home city. I started Wuhan Memory in the summer of 2026 because so many travel posts online are paid adverts that leave out whatever is bad about a place. Asking a large language model instead is easy, but the opening hours it gives, the time it says it takes to get between two places, and sometimes whether a place exists at all, can be made up, and they look just as convincing as the true ones.

Wuhan Memory splits the work. The model does what it is good at: understanding what the traveller says, and choosing and ordering places from a list it is given. Everything that has to be true comes from somewhere checkable: place information from a database where every entry has a source and a date, travel times from AMap route planning, and arrival and departure times worked out by the program. Before any itinerary is shown, the program checks it against that data. If it has errors, the model gets one chance to fix them. If it still fails, the trip is not shown; the user sees the list of problems.

Information that the program cannot confirm is not hidden or presented as fact. It stays in the trip, marked “to confirm”. Language models tend to guess rather than say “I don't know”; this label is how the system says it for them.

02 · From my statement to working softwareEach point, and where to check it

What I said, and what you can check

My personal statement describes this project. Below, each thing it says about the project is quoted on the left, with what exists now on the right and where to look for it.

  1. “If you type in, say, ‘I arrive on Friday evening, leave on Sunday evening, and I like history and local snacks’, the app comes back with a plan for every day and puts it on a map.”
    Built

    The map workbench (/map): a chat on the left, an AMap map in the middle, trip cards on the right. One sentence produces up to three plans with different emphases, drawn day by day on the map with numbered pins and real routes between stops. If the days or dates are missing, it asks. Works on phones too.

    apps/web/app/map/ · see the tour in section 03
  2. “I did the system design and the data model myself. The code was built by AI coding assistants from design documents I wrote, so those had to be really clear, and when the code came back I checked all of it.”
    Documented

    My project brief sets the requirements, the working rules and the order of work, block by block. The architecture, data model, API contracts and planning pipeline are each written up, and nine architecture decision records (ADRs) explain each major choice, its alternatives and its cost. Each block was built on its own branch and merged only after I had tried and accepted it. Section 07 describes how the work was divided.

    docs/kickoff/claude-code-kickoff.md · docs/architecture/ · docs/adr/ · docs/progress/dev-log.md
  3. “Right now it's on Amap (Gaode Maps), and my friends and family have had a go.”
    Built

    Maps use the AMap JavaScript API 2.0, with a 2D / 3D switch; routes for walking, bus and metro, and driving come from AMap's route planning service, called by the backend and cached with the date they were looked up. Friends and family trying the app is my own account; it isn't recorded in the repository.

    packages/map-core/ · apps/api/app/services/routing/
  4. “Each attraction needs to have its coordinates and a recorded source.”
    Enforced

    Each place is a JSON file, and every single fact in it points to a source: title, link, date read and type of source. A checking script refuses to import a place with missing coordinates, coordinates outside Wuhan, or a fact without a source.

    data/pois/ · apps/api/app/data_quality/ · section 05
  5. “For the sort of information that changes (e.g. opening hours and travel times) there also has to be a record of when it was last checked and when it expires.”
    Enforced

    Every changeable fact has lastCheckedAt and expiresAt, with maximum lifetimes: 90 days for opening hours and booking, 180 days for prices, payment and food, 365 days for transport. Cached travel times keep the date they were queried. Expired facts are labelled “expired” on the site.

    docs/architecture/data-model.md
  6. “No plan from the AI goes to a user until it's been checked against this data.”
    Built

    validate_itinerary checks every stop: does the place exist, is it open on arrival, is it a closing day, is it past last entry, can the visitor leave before closing, is the day too long, was the route found, and do the plan's rules hold. If there are errors the model gets one chance to fix them; a plan that still fails is not shown.

    apps/api/app/services/planning/validate.py · ADR 0004 · section 04
  7. “If there's something I can't confirm it stays in but with ‘unconfirmed’ written on it.”
    Built

    Every fact carries a verification status. Anything not yet confirmed is shown as “待确认” in Chinese and “to confirm” in English, and anything missing as “to fill in”, on place profiles, trip cards and share pages. In validation, missing or unconfirmed information is a warning, not an error, because “not recorded” doesn't mean “closed”.

    apps/api/app/services/planning/validate.py · /places
  8. “I designed a way to run two models side by side (Qwen and Doubao for instance) and compare the quality of the plans they come up with.”
    Built

    All model calls go through one LLMGateway, so Qwen and Doubao can be switched with one click. The comparison page (/compare) sends one request to both at the same time, with identical preferences, candidate places and travel data, and shows both trips with a scorecard computed by the program. A batch script runs a set of requests and writes result files.

    /compare · apps/api/app/services/llm/ · eval/ · ADR 0006 · section 06
  9. “In my database I've got notes like ‘checked last month’.”
    Built

    Each fact records the date it was last checked, shown as “Checked 2026.11.15” under the fact on its place profile. Today that date is shown as it is; turning it into a measure of how much to trust a record is something I'd like to learn to do.

    data/pois/ · /places/[id]
  10. “Their feedback was that the plans didn't feel new and that the logic behind what the AI was saying was quite simple.”
    Open problem

    This is my friends' feedback, as I described it. The database has 10 places, and adding places carefully is slow, so the model has few choices to work with. Each plan does give a reason for each stop, and three emphases make the plans differ by rule, but the planned next steps are reasons backed by evidence, alternatives for each stop, and more preferences.

    README.md, “Planned”
Also built, though not described in my statement: a Next.js frontend and FastAPI backend with 446 automated backend tests; a 2D / 3D map switch; payment hints for each place; read-only share pages; a list of saved trips with versions; a full English version of the site; a 3D darkroom-desk interface; and a “public mode” that protects the site and its model budget when other people use it.

04 · How it worksArchitecture and pipeline

Who does what

The system has a few hard boundaries. Business code never calls a model provider directly; it goes through the gateway. Pages never touch AMap objects directly; they use a map provider interface. SQL lives only in the repository layer, so SQLite can later be swapped for PostgreSQL. API keys for AMap's security code, routing, Qwen and Doubao stay on the backend; the browser only ever receives the AMap JavaScript key.

Simplified. The full diagram and each component are described in docs/architecture/system-architecture.md.

From one sentence to a checked itinerary

  1. ModelExtract preferences. Days, start date, pace, interests, budget, who is travelling, transport, must-see and must-avoid. If days or date are missing it asks back; anything else unsaid gets a default, and the trip says “by default”.
  2. ProgramPick candidates. From the place database, minus places the user rejected and places temporarily closed. The model may only use these.
  3. ProgramSet three emphases. “The classics” (all 5A-rated sights, unless the user named their own must-sees), “Easy, less walking” (at most 3 stops a day, finished by 17:30, under 2 km on foot), “Deep culture” (cultural places only, full suggested visit time). These are rules the program checks, not adjectives the model is asked to follow.
  4. ModelPlan. For each emphasis: which stops each day, in what order, and how long to stay. The prompt includes real travel times between every pair of candidates.
  5. ProgramLook up travel, compute the clock. Real AMap routes between consecutive stops (walk if under 15 minutes, otherwise transit or taxi). Arrival = previous departure + travel + 10 minutes, rounded up to 5 minutes; wait if the place isn't open yet.
  6. ProgramValidate. validate_itinerary checks every stop against the data and the emphasis rules, sorting findings into errors and warnings. Missing information is a warning, not an error: “not recorded” doesn't mean “closed”.
  7. BothFix once. If there are errors, the model receives each error, the computed times and the real travel times, and revises once. Then the clock is recomputed and validation runs again.
  8. ProgramShow or withhold, and save. Failing plans are not shown, only their problems; near-duplicate plans are merged. Each plan is saved as an unchangeable version with the model name, the validation result, the number of fix rounds and a snapshot of the place data it used.
05 · Data quality rulesEnforced by a script

Every fact has a source and a date

Each of the 10 places (Yellow Crane Tower, Hubei Provincial Museum, East Lake Tingtao, Wuhan University, Hubu Alley, Tanhualin, Lihuangpi Road, Jianghan Road Pedestrian Street, Hankou Riverside, Gude Temple) is one JSON file. Every fact inside it, from address and hours to tickets, booking, payment, transport, photo spots and nearby food, is recorded separately with:

FieldMeaning
verificationChecked on site · checked against source · placeholder · TODO
sourceIdPoints to the file's source list: title, link, date read, type of source
lastCheckedAtWhen it was last verified
expiresAtFor facts that change. Maximum: 90 days for hours and booking; 180 days for prices, payment and food; 365 days for transport

The checking script (pnpm check:data) treats these as errors that stop a place being imported: missing coordinates, coordinates outside Wuhan, a missing source, a missing check date or expiry date, an expiry beyond the maximum, a referenced photo file that doesn't exist. Expired facts are warnings: imported, but labelled “expired” on the site. The script has its own tests: one valid made-up place plus 12 copies that each break one rule, and every one must be caught.

Current state of the data, counted by the program: 185 facts across the 10 places. Checked against a source: 157. Placeholder: 16. TODO: 12. Expired: 0. On the site, placeholder facts are labelled “to confirm” and TODO facts “to fill in”. Some sources (for example Ctrip) refuse automated access, so their original text could not be compared by the program.
06 · Evaluating Qwen and DoubaoResults generated by script

Comparing models fairly

For the comparison to say anything about the models, everything except the model has to be the same. In the batch evaluation both models receive the same hand-written preferences (not extracted by a model, so both sides start identical), the same candidate places, the same emphasis and the same cached travel times, and are called at the same moment. Every metric is computed by the program. A run where a model failed to answer still counts in the denominator. I agreed these rules before running any comparison.

Passed on first draftPassed after one fix
Run 1 · model writes its own clock times10 runs per model · eval/results/2026-11-15.md
Qwen
2/10 first · 4/10 after fix Doubao
3/10 first · 7/10 after fix
Run 2 · real travel-time table added to the prompt30 runs per model · eval/results/2026-11-15-2.md
Qwen
5/30 first · 15/30 after fix Doubao
9/30 first · 18/30 after fix
Run 3 · the program computes clock times10 runs per model · eval/results/2026-11-15-3.md
Qwen
3/10 first · 8/10 after fix Doubao
5/10 first · 9/10 after fix

“Passed” means no errors; warnings don't count, since almost every trip still includes some “to confirm” information. The pipeline changed between runs, so the three runs should not be compared as if they were one experiment.

What the results showed

  • In the first run, the most common error for both models was “not enough travel time” between stops. Putting real travel times into the prompt (run 2) barely reduced it: the models still left round gaps of 15, 20 or 30 minutes. That result led to the decision to let the program compute clock times (section 07).
  • Neither model ever used a place outside the candidate list. Only 3 “invented places” appeared, all from Doubao in run 2, and all were the same misspelled ID (yellow-crape-tower for yellow-crane-tower), not an invented location.
  • In run 3, Qwen's remaining errors were mostly leaving out a 5A sight required by “the classics” and scheduling Hubei Provincial Museum on a Monday, when it is closed; Doubao's were mostly days that ran too long and leaving after closing time.
  • Average model time in run 3: Qwen 16.3 s, Doubao 13.2 s. Average tokens (in / out): Qwen 6,092 / 687, Doubao 5,498 / 524.
With only 10 requests and 10 places, mostly one run each, these numbers give a rough picture only. The metrics cover what a program can check, not whether a trip is enjoyable. So the evaluation does not conclude which model is better.
07 · My role and decisionsHow the work was divided

How I built it

The code was written by an AI coding assistant, Anthropic's Claude, working from my project brief. My part was the system design, the requirements, the design decisions and checking the results.

My brief sets out what the site must do, the rules the work must follow (never invent place information, never hard-code test results, never rewrite git history) and the order of the blocks. Before each piece of work, the assistant explained how it planned to do it, the possible approaches and the trade-offs of each, and I chose. Afterwards I tried it in the browser, looked at screenshots, or ran tests and evaluations in the terminal, and only then merged it. The process is recorded in a dated development log, and every major technical decision has its own ADR. Some of the decisions that shaped the project:

Order of work

Statement features first

I split the work into blocks and put the features from my statement first: data quality, model switching, validation and the model comparison. The 3D interface came last, so the core would exist even if time ran out.

ADR 0007

The program computes the clock

When adding real travel times to the prompt did not reduce timing errors, I chose, from three options the assistant laid out, to have the model decide only where, in what order and for how long. The program works out the times.

ADR 0006

Fair evaluation rules

Before comparing, I set the rules: inputs differ only in the model, calls are simultaneous, and failed runs count against the pass rate rather than being dropped.

ADR 0008

Protection before going public

A “public mode” for when others use the site: managing saved trips and share links needs a passcode, and planning is rate-limited so visitors can't use up the model budget.

ADR 0003

JSON + SQLite instead of PostgreSQL

My computer has no Docker, so I replaced the planned PostgreSQL + PostGIS with JSON seed files and SQLite, needing no installation, behind a repository layer so the database can be swapped later.

ADR 0005

Three plans with real differences

Instead of asking the model for “three different plans”, the program defines what each emphasis means and checks it, so the differences between plans are guaranteed by rules.

09 · LimitationsStated plainly

What isn't finished

  • Authorship. The code was written by an AI coding assistant, not line by line by me. I was responsible for the system design, requirements, design decisions and checking the results.
  • A small database. 10 places. Adding places carefully is slow, and with few places the plans have little room to be surprising.
  • Translations not reviewed. The English place texts were translated by Claude and have not been checked by a person.
  • Small evaluation. 10 requests, 10 places, mostly a single run each.
  • Not publicly hosted. The site runs on my computer. Steps for a temporary public link through a tunnel service are written up; permanent hosting is still being compared.
  • Planned next: collect place information faster while keeping it trustworthy; more planning abilities (where you're staying, meal breaks, editing an existing plan, reasons backed by evidence, alternatives for each stop); hosting; accounts.
